title: Dividing by five? Try doubling first
description: Turn a division by five into a doubling and a division by ten. See why it works, then try a few small puzzles.

cover.alt: Wooden counting tokens in small terracotta bowls on a linen table
cover.credit: AI-generated photorealistic illustration created for BrainiLab.

sections.title: How many groups of five?
sections.html:
You have 35 tokens and put five in each little bowl. How many bowls do you fill? Seven: five, ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five, thirty, thirty-five.

That is one meaning of 35 ÷ 5: how many groups of five fit into 35? If division still feels unfamiliar, begin with sharing and grouping. You do not need a trick to understand the question.

sections.title: Make the groups easier to count
sections.html:
Imagine making an identical copy of every token in every bowl. Each bowl now holds ten tokens instead of five. The total is 70, but there are still seven bowls.

So we can count groups of ten in 70 instead of groups of five in 35. We doubled both the total and the number in each group; the number of groups stayed the same.

That gives the shortcut: to divide by five, double the number and then divide by ten. For 85 ÷ 5, first double 85 to get 170. Then divide 170 by ten to get 17. Check it: 17 groups of five contain 85.

sections.title: Three bowls of practice
sections.html:
Try each one before opening the answer. Say the doubled number out loud if that helps you keep the two steps separate.

  1. 45 ÷ 5
  2. 120 ÷ 5
  3. 32 ÷ 5
Show the steps

45: double to 90, then divide by ten: 9.

120: double to 240, then divide by ten: 24.

32: double to 64, then divide by ten: 6.4. This last answer is not a whole number. If you only want complete groups of five tokens, you get six groups with two tokens left over.

sections.title: Useful shortcuts still need a check
sections.html:
Dividing by ten changes the place value; it does not mean “remove the last digit”. Removing the 4 from 64 would give the wrong answer. The decimal lesson shows what the dot is doing.

Number Route keeps division steps whole-number in its Easy format. The calculation 32 ÷ 5 is valid arithmetic, but it would not be an allowed step there. Understanding the game’s rule saves you from trying to force a decimal into a whole-number route.

Use the shortcut when it makes a calculation clearer. If you already know 25 ÷ 5 is 5, you can simply use that fact. A shortcut is a choice, not another rule to memorise before you are allowed to play.

practice: Try Number Route. Keep the numbers in order and check that each division leaves a whole number.
